q: Can an active customer hand over the installation, operation, data handling and maintenance of their equipment to an outside company, and does that company then count as an active customer itself?
answer: Yes. Active customers are entitled to delegate the management of the installations required for their activities, including installation, operation, data handling and maintenance, to a third party, and that third party is not considered an active customer (Article 15(2)(d)).

q: Until which date could countries still grant fresh entitlements to households under arrangements that offset what they inject against what they take off the mains, and may people already in them move to a different arrangement at any time?
answer: After 31 December 2023 no new rights may be granted under such schemes, and customers in existing schemes may at any time opt for a scheme that accounts separately for fed-in and consumed electricity as the basis for calculating network charges (Article 15(4)).

q: Are members of a citizen energy community free to leave it, and do they keep their rights as household or active customers while being members?
answer: Participation is open and voluntary, and members or shareholders are entitled to leave (in which case the supplier-switching rules of Article 12 apply); they do not lose their rights and obligations as household customers or active customers (Article 16(1)(a)-(c)).

q: Can a neighbourhood cooperative be given the right to run the local power lines in its area, and what must it agree with the larger grid company it is plugged into?
answer: Member States may grant citizen energy communities the right to manage distribution networks in their area; the community must then be entitled to conclude an agreement on the operation of its network with the distribution or transmission system operator to which its network is connected (Article 16(4)(a)).

q: Can a supplier charge penalties or impose other contractual restrictions on a customer because that customer signed up with an independent aggregator?
answer: No. The regulatory framework must provide that final customers with a contract with an independent aggregator are not subject to undue payments, penalties or other undue contractual restrictions by their suppliers (Article 17(3)(e)); the only payment Member States may allow is financial compensation strictly limited to the supplier's (or its balance responsible party's) costs caused by the activation of demand response (Article 17(4)).

q: How often must a distribution system operator refresh its published information on the capacity available for new connections, and within what time must it tell an applicant how their connection request is being handled?
answer: The capacity information must be updated at least quarterly; the operator must inform applicants about the status and treatment of their connection request within three months of submission, updating at least quarterly while the request is neither granted nor permanently rejected (Article 31(3)).

q: Can someone who wants to hook a new installation up to the local grid insist on sending the whole request and all supporting papers online only?
answer: Yes. Distribution system operators must give system users the option to request a grid connection and submit the relevant documents exclusively in digital form (Article 31(3a)).

q: How often must a distribution system operator publish its network development plan, and how far ahead must the planned investments reach?
answer: The plan must be published at least every two years and submitted to the regulatory authority; it sets out the planned investments for the next five to ten years (Article 32(3)).

q: May a distribution system operator own charging points for electric vehicles when they are only for its own company cars?
answer: Yes, but only private recharging points solely for its own use; otherwise distribution system operators may not own, develop, manage or operate recharging points for electric vehicles unless a Member State grants the derogation under paragraph 3 (Article 33(2)).

q: Can some of the statutory duties of a high-voltage grid manager be handed to another such company that does not hold title to the lines concerned, and what must that other company satisfy?
answer: Yes. Member States may assign one or several responsibilities to another TSO, which must be certified under the ownership unbundling, independent system operator or independent transmission operator model and meet the requirements of Article 43, but need not own the transmission system concerned (Article 40(2)).

q: How early may the update of input data used for day-ahead cross-zonal capacity calculation begin?
answer: The information update for the day-ahead time-frame may not start before 15:00 market time two days before the day of delivery; the calculation is based on the latest available information (Article 14(3)).

q: Under what conditions must two adjacent groupings of countries that both work out trading room with a power-flow model be fused into one?
answer: Flow-based capacity calculation regions must be merged if their transmission systems are directly linked, they take part in the same single day-ahead or intraday coupling area, and merging them is more efficient than keeping them separate (Article 15(3)).

q: Before a region switches to a different capacity calculation approach, for how long must the TSOs test the new approach alongside the existing one together with market participants?
answer: For at least six months before implementing a proposal for changing the capacity calculation approach (Article 20(8)).

q: Besides the standard method that simulates how power spreads through the network, which simpler way of working out trading room between price areas can grid companies ask regulators to apply, and what must they demonstrate?
answer: The coordinated net transmission capacity approach; the TSOs concerned must demonstrate that the flow-based approach would not yet be more efficient than it, assuming the same level of operational security in the region (Article 20(7)).

q: What must a method for working out cross-border trading room contain for the case in which the first computation produces no result at all?
answer: A fallback procedure for the case where the initial capacity calculation does not lead to any results (Article 21(3)).

q: In which two steps is the reliability margin for cross-zonal capacity determined?
answer: First the TSOs estimate the probability distribution of deviations between the expected power flows at the time of capacity calculation and the realised flows in real time; second the reliability margin is derived as a value from that distribution (Article 22(1)).

q: In flow-based capacity calculation, what does the available margin on a critical network element equal?
answer: The maximum flow on the element reduced by the adjusted flows (assuming no cross-zonal exchanges within the region), the reliability margin, and the flows resulting from previously allocated cross-zonal capacity, taking contingencies into account (Article 29(7)(e)).

q: When alternative price-area layouts are compared, what is required of the zone membership of each power plant or consumption unit at any given moment?
answer: Each generation and load unit must belong to only one bidding zone for each market time unit (Article 33(1)(c)(iii)).

q: By what date were the TSOs of each capacity calculation region to harmonise their redispatching and countertrading cost-sharing methodologies as far as possible between regions?
answer: By 31 December 2018 (Article 74(7)).

q: When already allocated long-term cross-zonal capacity must be curtailed, who validates the updated capacity figures that the coordinated capacity calculator comes up with?
answer: Each TSO validates the updated cross-zonal capacity on its own bidding zone borders or critical network elements (Article 25(4)).

q: Once the revised border trading room for cutting multi-year entitlements has been approved, to which central entity is it handed so that the cuts can be carried out?
answer: The coordinated capacity calculator provides the validated updated cross-zonal capacity to the relevant TSOs and to the single allocation platform, which performs the curtailment (Article 25(5)).

q: When a TSO curtails long-term transmission rights to stay within operational security limits, what must it tell the regulators and the public?
answer: It must report the curtailment to the respective regulatory authorities and publish the factual reasons that led to it (Article 53(1)).

q: What must a TSO make public when it cuts long-term transmission rights because of force majeure?
answer: A notification describing the nature of the force majeure and its probable duration (Article 56(2)).

q: Before cutting multi-year border entitlements because of an unforeseeable outside event, with whom must an operator liaise?
answer: The curtailment must be undertaken in a coordinated manner following liaison with all TSOs directly affected (Article 56(1)).

q: May a power store that a local grid firm has been permitted to run be used for trading on the market?
answer: No. Under the derogation, such facilities must be necessary for the distribution system operator's obligations and are not to be used to buy or sell electricity in the electricity markets (Article 36(2)(b)); the grandfathered batteries must likewise not be used for trading, including balancing (Article 36(4)(d)). Article 36 sets no such condition for fully integrated network components.

q: Do the remedial actions a TSO uses in real-time operation have to match those assumed in capacity calculation?
answer: Yes. The remedial actions used in system operation must be consistent with the remedial actions taken into account in capacity calculation (Article 20(2)).

q: What kinds of mishaps must a network operator anticipate before picking a countermeasure, such as those arising from rerouting lines or from output changes of plants?
answer: Risks of failure or short-circuit caused by topology changes, risks of outages caused by active or reactive power changes on generating modules or demand facilities, and risks of malfunction caused by equipment behaviour (Article 21(2)(c)).

q: What behaviour must the frequency restoration controller have in Continental Europe and the Nordic area, and what must its algorithm prevent?
answer: It must have proportional-integral behaviour, and its control algorithm must prevent the integral term from accumulating the control error and overshooting (Article 145(4)(b)-(c)).

q: How large is the reference incident for dimensioning frequency containment reserves in the Continental Europe synchronous area?
answer: 3 000 MW in the positive direction and 3 000 MW in the negative direction (Article 153(2)(b)(i)).

q: On what basis is each grid operator's first share of the fastest stabilising reserve duty split up within one interconnected area?
answer: On the sum of net generation and consumption of its control area divided by the sum of net generation and consumption of the whole synchronous area over a period of one year (Article 153(2)(d)).

q: What share of the required FCR may a single providing unit supply in the Continental Europe and Nordic synchronous areas?
answer: At most 5 % of the reserve capacity of FCR required for each of the whole Continental Europe and Nordic synchronous areas, i.e. of the FCR required for the synchronous area concerned (Article 156(6)(a)).

q: For how long at least must a battery with a small energy store keep fully delivering fast frequency support once the system is on the brink of trouble, if nothing else was agreed?
answer: At least 15 minutes (or a period set by each TSO that is neither shorter than 15 nor longer than 30 minutes) (Article 156(9)).

q: By how much may a load-frequency control block cut its positive FRR capacity through a sharing agreement in Continental Europe and the Nordic area?
answer: The reduction is limited to the difference, if positive, between the positive dimensioning incident and the FRR capacity needed to cover positive imbalances 99 % of the time, and may not exceed 30 % of the size of the positive dimensioning incident (Article 157(2)(j)(i)).

q: How much past imbalance history has to be consulted when deciding how much slower back-up power a control zone must keep available in Continental Europe and Scandinavia?
answer: Consecutive historical records of LFC block imbalances covering at least one full year, ending not earlier than 6 months before the calculation date (Article 157(2)(a)).

q: Within how many seconds must a resource that obeys the self-acting rebalancing signal begin to respond?
answer: The automatic FRR activation delay of an FRR providing unit or group may not exceed 30 seconds (Article 158(1)(d)).

q: What majority do TSOs need to adopt a pan-European methodology proposal when they cannot reach agreement?
answer: A qualified majority: TSOs representing at least 55 % of the Member States and Member States comprising at least 65 % of the population of the Union (Article 4(3)).

q: How often must grid operators send regulators a detailed account of the money spent on setting up and running the continent-wide balancing trading schemes?
answer: Yearly; all TSOs provide a yearly report explaining in detail the costs of establishing, amending and operating the platforms, which the Agency publishes (Article 23(1)).

q: For a grid operator that runs plants from a central control room, what is the longest lead time up to delivery at which the cut-off for revising plant-level offers may be placed?
answer: The integrated scheduling process gate closure time must be no longer than eight hours before real time, and set before the TSO energy bid submission gate closure time (Article 24(5)(b)-(c)).

q: How often do TSOs have to review the list of standard balancing products?
answer: At least every two years, taking into account the objectives of the Regulation, proposed changes to the number of common merit order lists and the performance indicators (Article 25(3)).

q: May a TSO modify or withhold the balancing energy bids it forwards to the activation optimisation function?
answer: No, except for bids covered by Articles 26 and 27, manifestly erroneous bids with an unfeasible delivery volume, and bids not forwarded to the European platforms under the volume-limiting proposal of paragraph 10 (Article 29(9)).

q: In which situations may balancing offers be called up before their cut-off time?
answer: In the alert or emergency state, when the activation helps alleviate the severity of those states, and when the bids serve purposes other than balancing (Article 29(2)).

q: Which kind of offers for regulating power must never fix the single uniform payment level when they are used to relieve bottlenecks inside the operator's own territory?
answer: Balancing energy bids activated for internal congestion management shall not set the marginal price of balancing energy (Article 30(1)(b)).

q: How often must the TSOs of a load-frequency control block review and define the reserve capacity they need?
answer: Regularly and at least once a year, pursuant to the dimensioning rules of the system operation guideline (Article 32(1)).

q: When grid operators pool offers for holding back standby power across borders, may they hold back or alter standard-product offers?
answer: No. All TSOs exchanging balancing capacity must submit all balancing capacity bids from standard products to the capacity procurement optimisation function and may not modify or withhold them, except under the conditions of Articles 26 and 27 (Article 33(3)).

q: What is the latest implementation date for the proposal that harmonises how imbalances are calculated and priced?
answer: No later than eighteen months after approval by all relevant regulatory authorities (Article 52(4)).

q: When a market participant's deviation from its trading plan is written as a minus number, does that mean it came up short or ended up with extra?
answer: A negative sign indicates the balance responsible party's shortage and a positive sign its surplus (Article 54(6)).

q: How must balance responsibility be defined for each connection in the terms and conditions for balance responsible parties?
answer: In a way that avoids any gaps or overlaps in the balance responsibility of the different market participants providing services to that connection (Article 18(6)(a)).

q: Must every power producer be responsible, directly or indirectly, for selling the electricity it generates?
answer: Yes. It is a principle of electricity market operation that all producers are directly or indirectly responsible for selling the electricity they generate (Article 3(k)).

q: From when before day-ahead gate closure must NEMOs send all their day-ahead orders to the single coupling and stop trading such products elsewhere?
answer: From one hour before the gate closure time until the latest point in time where day-ahead trade is allowed (Article 7(2)(ca)).

q: By when must the Commission assess possible changes to the maturities of long-term transmission rights, and how long might those maturities be extended?
answer: By 17 January 2026 the Commission must carry out an impact assessment that covers, among other things, maturities extended up to at least three years (Article 9(4)(b)).

q: Which central body hands out multi-year cross-border entitlements on behalf of grid operators, and what legal form must it have?
answer: The single allocation platform, which offers allocation and facilitates the trading of long-term transmission rights on behalf of TSOs; it must have a legal form as referred to in Annex II to Directive (EU) 2017/1132 (Article 9(7)).

q: For how long at most can the Commission approve a scheme that pays power plants for being available?
answer: For no longer than 10 years, and the committed capacities must be reduced on the basis of the implementation plan (Article 21(8)).

q: When a reserve of plants held outside the market is called on, at what price must the resulting market deviations be settled?
answer: At least at the value of lost load or at a higher value than the intraday technical price limit, whichever is higher (Article 22(2)(b)).

q: Does asking for a review of a coordinated action issued by a regional coordination centre suspend that action?
answer: No, except where implementing the action would violate the operational security limits defined by an individual TSO (Article 42(5)).

q: How is the volume of electricity transiting a country's high-voltage grid established when its operators receive reimbursement for carrying other countries' power?
answer: On the basis of the physical flows of electricity actually measured during a given period (Article 49(5)).

q: How often must derogations from basing balancing capacity procurement on a primary market be reviewed?
answer: Every three years (Article 6(8)).

q: If a regulator allows standby power to be bought far in advance or for extended stretches, what share of the offerings must still be bought at most a day before and for at most a day?
answer: At least 40 % of the standard balancing products and a minimum of 30 % of all products used for balancing capacity must be contracted no more than one day before provision, for a period of no more than one day (Article 6(9)).

q: Can a special grid fee be levied on an individual trade across a price-area border?
answer: No. There shall be no specific network charge on individual transactions for cross-zonal trading of electricity (Article 18(6)).

q: What happens to a market participant that fails to use the cross-border capacity it was allocated?
answer: It loses its rights to that capacity and must pay a cost-reflective charge that is justified and proportionate (Article 16(12)); capacity that will not be used must be made available again to the market (Article 16(10)).

q: May a sale of scarce border room between countries set a floor under what bidders may offer?
answer: No. Establishing reserve prices in capacity-allocation methods is prohibited, other than for new interconnectors that benefit from an exemption (Article 16(6)).
